newsitem.title: USA: Republicans work to shore up support for Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Republicans work to shore up support for Gingrich.

text.p: A second Republican lawmaker Friday publicly called for House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich to step down, even as party leaders sought to shore up support for Gingrich, who last month admitted he violated House ethics rules.

Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour led counter-attacks against Democrats as he and others scoffed at reports that Gingrich's support was eroding, predicting he would be re-elected with almost unanimous party backing.

But Representative Matt Salmon of Arizona spoke out on the CNN and ABC networks, saying Gingrich's ability to lead the House was compromised and the Georgia Republican should step down at least temporarily until the ethics charges were resolved.
"The honourable and right thing to do is for Newt Gingrich to step down, at least temporarily, until this can be resolved," Salmon told CNN's "Inside Politics."
He told ABC Gingrich called him personally Friday in an attempt to change his mind. Representative Michael Forbes, a Republican from New York, has also called for Gingrich to step down.

House Republicans were invited to join in a conference call to hear from Representative Steve Schiff of New Mexico, a member of an ethics panel that conducted a two-year investigation of ethics complaints against the speaker.

Schiff and his Republican colleague on the subcommittee, Porter Goss of Florida, said in a letter last week they would vote for Gingrich at next Tuesday's speakership election and knew of no reason why he would be ineligible to serve.
Twelve of 27 Republicans identified as "undecided" by the New York Times issued a letter late Friday saying they would also vote to re-elect Gingrich.

The vote on the speaker will take place as Congress reconvenes one day before the House Ethics Committee begins the last phase of a Gingrich investigation that will result in a recommendation to the full House on punishment.
Speculation has been that the committee will recommend a reprimand, a lesser punishment than expulsion or censure and one that would likely enable Gingrich to keep his post.

Republican leaders will press the case for his re-election in weekend television interview programmes and Gingrich himself will appear before all House Republicans at a meeting Monday night that could be crucial in nailing down their support.
Barbour, at a news conference, unleashed a tirade against Democrats, apparently as part of a strategy to make Gingrich's re-election an issue of party loyalty.

Accusing Democrats of trying to delay the ethics process so as to prevent Gingrich's re-election, Barbour said: "This is just a raw political power play. This is a shot by the Democrats to try to win by manipulating the ethics process that which they couldn't win at the ballot box."
He called the findings against Gingrich "very insignificant."

Gingrich on Dec. 21 agreed with the finding of the ethics subcommittee that he had given investigators false information and failed to ensure that he complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt donations for partisan purposes.
But Gingrich said he been "in some ways naive" and had not intended to mislead the committee.

Barbour compared the findings against Gingrich with the ethics panel's action on a complaint against House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt, saying both had submitted inaccurate information but Gephardt was let off with a letter of warning.

Last September the committee -- equally divided between Republicans and Democrats and with a Republican chairman -- dismissed a Republican-filed complaint alleging Gephardt had violated tax and banking laws in connection with his ownership of a second home.
The committee chided him for delaying and amending income statements and said he should be more diligent in the future.

Both Barbour and other Republican officials scoffed at a New York Times report that 27 Republicans were unwilling to commit themselves to voting for Gingrich, Barbour calling the report, "the rankest sort of speculation."
Republicans have a House majority of 227 to 207 Democrats and one independent who usually votes with the Democrats. The narrow majority means Gingrich can afford few defections.
